title: When the Sea Turns Cold, Rescuers Rush to Save Sea Turtles
summary:
On a cold December afternoon in 2025, Annemarie O'Connell went to a beach in Truro, Massachusetts, near the tip of Cape Cod, with a flashlight to look for sea turtles that had washed up, too cold to swim.

Sea turtles are reptiles, so they cannot make their own body heat. They feel best in water from 17 to 29 degrees Celsius (62 to 85 degrees Fahrenheit). But if the water drops below 10 degrees Celsius (50 degrees Fahrenheit) before they swim south, turtles can get too cold. They grow weak and slow. Some stop swimming and float at the surface. This is called cold stunning, and it leaves turtles dazed and numb.

Every winter, hundreds of cold-stunned turtles wash up on Massachusetts beaches. Many could not get past Cape Cod. Without help, they may die, but if they reach special hospitals quickly, many survive. Near high tide, O'Connell found a large loggerhead about one meter (three feet) long. "It was huge," O'Connell said. Helpers slid it onto a sled and drove it to care.
why_it_matters: Just like you need a warm coat on a freezing day, sea turtles need warm water and quick help to stay alive when winter makes the sea too cold for them.

Because sea turtles are reptiles and cannot make their own body heat
Because sea turtles drink too much cold seawater

background_read: Sea turtles are reptiles, so they cannot warm their own bodies and need warm water to stay active and healthy.
When the water gets too cold before they swim south, they can become cold-stunned, which means they grow weak, slow, and numb and may float at the surface.
That is why helpers look for washed-up turtles on beaches and take them to special hospitals, where many can recover.

WHY: The water had dropped below 10 degrees Celsius, leaving the turtle dazed and numb, so it needed quick help to survive
